cooling_items.text:
The building is not equipped with a centralized cooling system. Cooling within individual suites is provided by a combination of window-mounted air conditioners and portable indoor air-conditioning units.

These decentralized cooling devices are generally less efficient than modern centralized or heat-pump-based systems. Typical window and portable air-conditioning units operate with relatively low coefficients of performance (COP), often below 3.0, compared to high-efficiency heat pump systems which can achieve COP values exceeding 4.5–5.0 under favorable conditions.

In addition to reduced cooling efficiency, window-mounted air-conditioning units can negatively impact building envelope performance. Improper sealing around window installations may allow uncontrolled air infiltration during the heating season, increasing heat loss, draft complaints, and overall space-heating energy consumption. Installation of a air source heat pump (ASHP) system could be considered in a short term to mid term.
cooling_items.title: Window A/C Units

dhw_items.text:
The domestic hot water (DHW) system currently consists of two (2) RBI glass-lined water heaters installed approximately five (5) years ago as part of a previous retrofit. Each unit has an estimated storage capacity of approximately 200 gallons and is heated via the central DHW boiler.

Based on feedback from property management and tenant complaints, the current DHW system is undersized and unable to meet peak domestic hot water demand, resulting in frequent instances of insufficient hot water availability.

An existing large-capacity DHW storage tank, likely original to the building (circa 1970s), remains in the mechanical room but is currently disconnected from the system. The tank has recently undergone internal cleaning; however, insulation reline has not yet been completed at the time of site visit. No nameplate was observed on the tank. Based on field observation and dimensional estimation, the storage capacity is approximately 1,000–1,200 gallons.

Overall, the current system relies primarily on relatively small-volume storage tanks, with limited buffering capacity, contributing to poor performance during peak demand periods.
dhw_items.title: Aging indirect tank + RBI water heater

dhw_items.text:
One (1) indirect storage tank was observed, located at the main boiler room and is heated via DHW boiler. The tank was observed to be in fair mechanical condition.

Aging indirect tanks typically require periodic internal relining and ongoing maintenance to maintain performance and water quality. As these components continue to age, maintenance requirements and the risk of unplanned service interruptions are expected to increase.
dhw_items.title: Indirect storage tank

dhw_items.title: Mechanical Mixing valves

dhw_items.text: The existing DHW boiler failed because the current piping arrangement introduces cold water directly into the return side, creating condensing conditions that damaged the non-condensing heat exchanger; replacement with a similar-capacity condensing boiler is recommended because the existing piping is well suited for condensing operation.
dhw_items.title: Failed DHW Boiler Observed

heating_items.text:
Space heating within individual suites is provided through a decentralized electric resistance heating system consisting of electric baseboard heaters and radiant ceiling heating panels.

The radiant ceiling system utilizes embedded electric heating elements within the ceiling assembly to provide heat through thermal radiation to interior spaces. Electric baseboard heaters provide supplementary convective heating as required. Each suite is equipped with wall-mounted thermostats, allowing occupants to manually control space temperature.

This configuration provides basic suite-level temperature control; however, electric resistance heating operates at a coefficient of performance (COP) of approximately 1.0, resulting in relatively high electrical energy consumption compared to modern heat pump–based systems. In addition, the absence of centralized monitoring, scheduling, or optimization limits opportunities for system-wide energy management and may contribute to inconsistent comfort conditions across suites.
heating_items.title: Ceiling heating

heating_items.text: In Common areas, additional heating and cooling are provided by ceiling-mounted 4-way ceiling cassette indoor unit units. These units provide localized conditioning to maintain occupant comfort in high-traffic areas and are integrated within the ceiling space.
heating_items.title: Common area space heating

measures.existing_conditions: The existing HVAC mechanical systems—including MUAs, exhaust fans, heating boilers, DHW plant, cooling equipment, and pumps—are controlled manually or via basic local thermostats and temperature sensors. There is minimal outdoor-air reset, limited boiler sequencing, and no centralized scheduling or monitoring. Equipment often operates during unoccupied periods, leading to excessive energy use and chronic overheating.
measures.notes: Install a new central BAS to Control boilers, DHW, MUAs, pumps and exhaust fans with scheduling, reset and remote access, reducing energy use and maintenance. Improve building operation and management.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
It is recommended to install a centralized BAS to control all major HVAC systems. The BAS would provide occupancy-based scheduling, outdoor-temperature reset for boilers, zone-level temperature modulation, real-time monitoring, remote access, and alarm notifications. Improved control will reduce unnecessary run time, lower energy consumption, and improve comfort while reducing maintenance costs through better diagnostics. Utility incentives for advanced building controls can further improve project economics, with typical paybacks on the order of 3–4 years.

*Where applicable, IESO incentives and Enbridge incentives for central heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics. Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/100-000-enbridge-incentive

measures.existing_conditions: The building is served by a single interval meter and there is currently no electrical sub-metering system in place to monitor power distribution or track the electricity use of individual tenants or loads.
measures.notes: Install certified electrical sub-meters on main feeds to enable consumption-based billing and end-use tracking, typically driving 5–30% electricity savings per suite.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to install an electrical sub-metering system to measure electricity use by tenant or by major end-use. Certified sub-meters would be installed on the main feeds in electrical closets and programmed to track usage for each unit or load. Sub-metering enables fair, consumption-based billing and encourages occupants to reduce waste, typically resulting in 5–30% electricity savings per suite. Measurement Canada certified meters ensure accuracy and tamper resistance, making this a practical solution for existing multi-unit buildings where full utility meter replacement is not feasible.

measures.existing_conditions:
The domestic hot water (DHW) system is currently served by a non-condensing gas-fired boiler that has been damaged and is no longer able to operate reliably. Based on site review and piping arrangement, cold domestic water is being introduced directly into the return-water side of the existing DHW boiler. This condition substantially lowers the entering water temperature to the boiler.

While lower return-water temperatures can improve efficiency in a condensing boiler application, the existing DHW boiler is a non-condensing unit and is not designed to operate below the flue-gas dew point. As a result, sustained flue-gas condensation likely occurred within the heat exchanger, leading to internal deterioration and premature damage to the boiler. In effect, the current piping configuration is unsuitable for the existing non-condensing boiler, but is inherently favorable for condensing boiler operation.
measures.measure_title: Replace DHW Boiler with Condensing Boiler
measures.notes: Replace the failed non-condensing DHW boiler with a new condensing boiler of similar capacity, using the existing low-return-temperature piping configuration to improve efficiency and restore reliable domestic hot water service.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends replacing the failed existing DHW boiler with a new high-efficiency condensing boiler of similar heating capacity. A condensing boiler is specifically designed to operate with low return-water temperatures and recover latent heat from the flue gases, making it well suited to the current piping configuration.

Under the proposed retrofit, the new condensing boiler would be installed and integrated with the existing DHW system, while maintaining the piping arrangement that currently promotes low return-water temperatures. This would allow the replacement boiler to operate within its intended condensing range, improving thermal efficiency, reducing natural gas consumption, and restoring reliable DHW service.

In addition to improved energy performance, this retrofit would better align the equipment selection with the actual hydronic conditions observed on site, reducing the risk of repeat heat-exchanger damage associated with improper boiler application.

measures.existing_conditions:
The current DHW system consists of two (2) RBI glass-lined water heaters (~200 gallons each) supplied by a central DHW boiler. The existing system has been reported by property management to be undersized, with frequent hot water shortages during peak demand.

One (1) DHW boiler is currently non-operational due to internal damage associated with low return-water temperature conditions. In addition, an existing large-capacity storage tank (circa 1970s) remains disconnected. While recently cleaned, the tank is aged, lacks identification/nameplate, and has not been reinsulated at the time of site visit.

The current system configuration does not provide sufficient storage capacity or optimized hydraulic arrangement to support peak DHW demand or stable system operation.
measures.measure_title: Replace Aging DHW Storage Tank and piping and Condensing DHW Boiler Retrofit
measures.notes: Replace the failed DHW boiler with a new condensing unit and increase system capacity by adding additional RBI storage water heaters, eliminating aging storage tanks and improving both reliability and hot water availability.

measures.existing_conditions:
Space heating within the building is currently provided by electric resistance systems, including radiant ceiling heating panels and baseboard heaters. These systems operate independently within each suite and are controlled by local thermostats.

Electric resistance heating operates at a coefficient of performance (COP) of approximately 1.0, resulting in relatively high electrical energy consumption during the heating season. In addition, the radiant ceiling heating system is embedded within the building structure, limiting maintainability and flexibility for future upgrades. The current system also does not provide cooling capability and offers limited opportunities for centralized control or optimization.
measures.measure_title: Transition electric resistance heating system to Mini-Split Heat Pump Systems
measures.notes: Transition from electric resistance heating to high-efficiency mini-split heat pump systems to reduce energy consumption, improve comfort, and provide integrated heating and cooling capability.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends transitioning the existing electric resistance heating systems to high-efficiency ductless mini-split heat pump systems. The proposed system would provide both heating and cooling within each suite through wall-mounted or ceiling-mounted indoor units connected to outdoor condensing units.

Mini-split heat pumps operate by transferring heat rather than generating it, achieving typical heating COP values in the range of 2.5 to 4.0 or higher depending on outdoor conditions. This significantly reduces electrical consumption compared to resistance-based systems while also providing integrated cooling capability.

The retrofit may include:

Installation of ductless indoor units within each suite
Installation of outdoor condensing units (roof or exterior wall mounted)
Electrical upgrades as required to support new equipment
Removal or decommissioning of existing electric resistance heating systems where feasible

This transition improves overall energy efficiency, reduces operating costs, enhances occupant comfort, and supports long-term building electrification and decarbonization strategies.

*Further engineering review and detailed feasibility study are required to confirm system design, electrical capacity, equipment layout, and installation approach.

For additional information regarding electrification strategies and retrofit support, please visit:
https://www.mannengineering.com/ask-an-energy-expert

measures.existing_conditions: The building is served by a make-up air (MUA) unit equipped with a gas-fired heating section and fixed or limited-speed supply fan control. The unit provides ventilation air to corridors and common areas but relies primarily on natural gas combustion for winter heating. While the system is functional, gas-fired heating results in ongoing fuel consumption and limits opportunities for electrification and high-efficiency operation.
measures.measure_title: Retrofit Existing MUA to ASHP MUA with VFD (Gas Heating as Backup)
measures.notes: Upgrade the MUA to a Hybrid MUA with VFD control while retaining gas heating as backup to reduce gas use and improve energy performance. Qualify for Enbridge incentives.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends retrofitting the existing MUA unit to operate as an air source heat pump (ASHP) MUA system while retaining the existing gas-fired heating section as a backup for extreme cold-weather conditions. Under the proposed configuration, an ASHP heating and cooling section would be integrated into the existing MUA cabinet (subject to engineering review), allowing the unit to provide high-efficiency heating and cooling through a refrigeration cycle.

New or upgraded variable frequency drives (VFDs) would be installed on the supply fan to enable airflow modulation based on ventilation demand and discharge air temperature requirements. Integration into a Building Automation System (BAS), where available, would allow optimized scheduling, temperature reset, and coordinated system control.

The ASHP system would handle the majority of annual heating and cooling loads, significantly reducing natural gas consumption, while the existing gas-fired section would operate only as supplemental or emergency heat. This hybrid approach improves energy efficiency, supports decarbonization goals, and minimizes capital cost by retaining functional components of the existing unit.

*This measure is recommended subject to a detailed feasibility study to confirm equipment sizing, electrical service capacity, structural considerations, and integration constraints. The existing gas-fired heating section is recommended to be retained as backup to ensure reliability and operational flexibility.

*Where applicable, IESO and Enbridge incentives for heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics. Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/100-000-enbridge-incentive

measures.existing_conditions: At the present, the building relies on external utilities to provide electricity to power the building which might lead to high electrical energy costs.
measures.notes: Install net metered solar PV generated electricity to offset electricity consumption.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
The current state of the solar industry in Ontario is focused on “net metering” as power export to the grid is no longer an option. Rather than power export, net metered solar facilities use the generated electricity to offset electricity consumption within the facility. Since power export is not feasible, the system should be sized to only meet the baseload energy consumption of the building. This building has a high electrical consumption and ample roof space, which makes it a candidate for solar PV. 

A preliminary study is required to accurately estimate the system cost and savings for a Solar PV system

measures.existing_conditions: The building’s electrical infrastructure is currently operating near or at its available capacity, with limited allowance for additional electrical loads. The existing transformer and distribution system were designed based on historical building demand and may not be adequate to support modern electrification strategies or increased plug and HVAC loads.
measures.notes: Upgrade electrical infrastructure capacity to enable future electrification, including heat pump systems, EV charging, and other high-efficiency electrical upgrades.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends conducting a comprehensive electrical system upgrade strategy to improve the building’s capacity for future electrification and energy-efficiency retrofits. This may include:

Installation of additional transformer capacity or replacement with higher-capacity units
Upgrades to main distribution panels and feeders
Load redistribution and panel balancing
Integration planning for future electrified systems such as air-source heat pumps (ASHP), EV charging infrastructure, and high-efficiency electric equipment

Improving electrical infrastructure capacity will enable the building to transition toward lower-carbon technologies, support future HVAC upgrades, and enhance long-term operational flexibility.

*Further engineering review and detailed feasibility study are required to confirm system capacity, infrastructure constraints, and implementation strategy.

*For additional information regarding electrification strategies and retrofit support, please visit:
https://www.mannengineering.com/ask-an-energy-expert

measures.existing_conditions: Electric vehicle (EV) ownership is expected to grow substantially over the next decade, and many multi-residential and commercial buildings currently lack dedicated EV charging infrastructure for residents, staff, or visitors
measures.notes: Plan and install EV charging infrastructure for residents and staff, contact us for more detail.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Upgrading through the Trade‑In Program is recommended to replace outdated units with OCPP‑networked TAR‑M chargers, providing managed access, usage metering, and load balancing. Early participants benefit from reduced capital cost, including no‑cost upgrades for the first two owners, along with ongoing carbon‑credit rebates of $0.03–$0.05/kWh.

*Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/

misc_items.text:
The building is currently served by an existing electrical transformer rated at approximately 416 V / 75 kVA, which appears undersized relative to current building demand. Based on discussions with the ESA technician, the existing transformer capacity is insufficient to support additional electrical loads, and installation of an additional transformer of similar capacity would be required to accommodate future demand.

This limitation restricts the building’s ability to implement future electrification measures, including but not limited to air-source heat pump (ASHP) retrofits or other electrically driven HVAC system upgrades.
misc_items.title: Electrical Capacity Limitation – Transformer

misc_items.text: The building appears to be served by a single master interval meter, and there is currently no electrical sub-metering system in place to monitor power distribution or track electricity consumption at the individual suite or major end-use level. Based on discussions with site staff, utility costs, including hydro and domestic hot water, are incorporated into common maintenance fees, which suggests that consumption is not individually metered.
misc_items.title: No sub-metering

misc_items.text: The parking garage is served by a mechanical ventilation system controlled by carbon monoxide (CO) sensors. Exhaust fans start and stop in response to measured CO levels, providing demand-based operation and reducing unnecessary runtime during periods of low vehicle activity. The garage fans and control system appeared to be functioning normally, with no obvious mechanical deficiencies reported.
misc_items.title: Garage ventilation (Has CO controls)

misc_items.text: The building envelope appears to be in generally good condition, with no significant signs of air leakage or deterioration observed at the time of the site visit. Envelope components appear to be performing as intended.
misc_items.title: Envelope Condition (Good)

misc_items.text: Lighting throughout the building is generally in good working order. Common areas, corridors, and service spaces appear to be equipped with a mix of LED and fluorescent fixtures. No widespread outages were observed during the walkthrough, and the overall lighting levels were appropriate for the building’s use. Further savings may be available through continued LED retrofit and the use of occupancy-based controls in selected low-traffic areas. Or installing light control in the parking area.
misc_items.title: Lighting condition and controls

misc_items.text: In aging buildings, even double-pane window assemblies may experience gradual deterioration of glazing seals over time. Loss of insulating gas or degradation of the sealed air space between panes can reduce overall thermal performance. While the existing windows were observed to be in generally fair condition, it would be prudent to incorporate sealant renewal and eventual glazing upgrades into the building’s long-term capital planning strategy.
misc_items.title: Window condition (Aging double pane)

misc_items.text: The existing toilets are estimated to operate at approximately 4.8 liters per flush (LPF). Upgrading to modern dual-flush, low-flow toilet fixtures, typically rated at approximately 3.0–3.5 LPF for full flush with reduced volumes for liquid waste, would reduce domestic water consumption and associated sewer charges while maintaining acceptable fixture performance and occupant comfort.
misc_items.title: Toilet Flush (4.8 LPF)

misc_items.text: The building includes an unheated parking garage, which is typical for buildings of this age. No dedicated space-heating system was observed, and garage temperatures are allowed to fluctuate with outdoor conditions.
misc_items.title: Unheated garage

misc_items.text: The exterior ramp heating system is hydronic ramp heating and is used to maintain safe, ice-free conditions during winter months. No operational issues were observed with the ramp heating system at the time of the visit. Control improvements may be possible by converting the electric ramp heating system to a hydronic system, where feasible, to reduce electrical energy consumption while maintaining winter safety performance
misc_items.title: Electric ramp heating

misc_items.text: The building is served by a packaged domestic water booster pump system equipped with variable frequency drives (VFDs). The booster pack modulates pump speed in response to system demand, maintaining stable water pressure throughout the building while reducing unnecessary energy consumption during low-demand periods. The booster pump system was observed to be operating normally at the time of the site visit, with no abnormal noise, vibration, or visible mechanical deficiencies noted
misc_items.title: Has VFD on Booster Pump

misc_items.text: The indoor pool area is served by a dedicated dehumidifer providing ventilation, dehumidification, and space conditioning. The unit is designed to control humidity levels, maintain indoor air quality, and prevent condensation-related deterioration within the pool enclosure
misc_items.title: Pool dehumidifer

misc_items.text: No emergency generator was observed on site. Stairwell emergency lighting is supported by a battery backup system consisting of approximately ten (10) batteries. While this configuration provides basic life-safety lighting during power outages, it does not support extended backup power for other critical building systems.
misc_items.title: No Emergency Generator

misc_items.text: The building is served by aging in suite fuse panels consistent with the original construction era. While the panel appeared to be functional and no immediate safety deficiencies were observed during the site visit, its configuration and capacity reflect outdated electrical standards and may offer limited flexibility to support future electrical loads, energy-efficiency upgrades, or electrification initiatives. Further detailed electrical assessment is recommended prior to implementing major electrical or energy-related retrofits to confirm available capacity, code compliance, and long-term suitability
misc_items.title: Electric Panel (fuse panels)

ventilation_items.text: Ventilation for the building is provided by two (2) make-up air (MUA) units, located in roof top, serving corridors and other public areas.
ventilation_items.title: Rooftop MUA

ventilation_items.text:
The existing make-up air (MUA) unit is equipped with a constant-speed supply fan and an integral gas-fired heating burner, providing heating-only capacity. The unit does not include variable frequency drive (VFD) control and does not provide mechanical cooling.

The absence of VFD control results in fixed airflow operation regardless of actual ventilation demand, limiting part-load efficiency and increasing electrical energy consumption. The gas-fired heating section provides basic winter heating capability; however, without cooling capacity, heat recovery, or advanced modulation control, the system offers limited seasonal optimization and indoor temperature regulation.

At the time of the site visit, the unit was observed to be in functional condition with no visible mechanical deficiencies. However, the configuration reflects an older, conventional ventilation design with limited energy efficiency and control flexibility.
ventilation_items.title: No VFD + Gas Fire (heating only)

Heating Plant Issue: No VFD on Suite Circulation Pumps

measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends transitioning the existing electric resistance heating systems to high-efficiency ductless mini-split heat pump systems. The proposed system would provide both heating and cooling within each suite through wall-mounted or ceiling-mounted indoor units connected to outdoor condensing units.

Mini-split heat pumps operate by transferring heat rather than generating it, achieving typical heating COP values in the range of 2.5 to 4.0 or higher depending on outdoor conditions. This significantly reduces electrical consumption compared to resistance-based systems while also providing integrated cooling capability.

The retrofit may include:

Installation of ductless indoor units within each suite
Installation of outdoor condensing units (roof or exterior wall mounted)
Electrical upgrades as required to support new equipment
Removal or decommissioning of existing electric resistance heating systems where feasible

This transition improves overall energy efficiency, reduces operating costs, enhances occupant comfort, and supports long-term building electrification and decarbonization strategies.

*Further engineering review and detailed feasibility study are required to confirm system design, electrical capacity, equipment layout, and installation approach.

For additional information regarding electrification strategies and retrofit support, please visit:
https://www.mannengineering.com/ask-an-energy-expert

measures.existing_conditions: The building is served by a make-up air (MUA) unit equipped with a gas-fired heating section and fixed or limited-speed supply fan control. The unit provides ventilation air to corridors and common areas but relies primarily on natural gas combustion for winter heating. While the system is functional, gas-fired heating results in ongoing fuel consumption and limits opportunities for electrification and high-efficiency operation.
measures.measure_title: Retrofit Existing MUA to ASHP MUA with VFD (Gas Heating as Backup)
measures.notes: Upgrade the MUA to a Hybrid MUA with VFD control while retaining gas heating as backup to reduce gas use and improve energy performance. Qualify for Enbridge incentives.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends retrofitting the existing MUA unit to operate as an air source heat pump (ASHP) MUA system while retaining the existing gas-fired heating section as a backup for extreme cold-weather conditions. Under the proposed configuration, an ASHP heating and cooling section would be integrated into the existing MUA cabinet (subject to engineering review), allowing the unit to provide high-efficiency heating and cooling through a refrigeration cycle.

New or upgraded variable frequency drives (VFDs) would be installed on the supply fan to enable airflow modulation based on ventilation demand and discharge air temperature requirements. Integration into a Building Automation System (BAS), where available, would allow optimized scheduling, temperature reset, and coordinated system control.

The ASHP system would handle the majority of annual heating and cooling loads, significantly reducing natural gas consumption, while the existing gas-fired section would operate only as supplemental or emergency heat. This hybrid approach improves energy efficiency, supports decarbonization goals, and minimizes capital cost by retaining functional components of the existing unit.

*This measure is recommended subject to a detailed feasibility study to confirm equipment sizing, electrical service capacity, structural considerations, and integration constraints. The existing gas-fired heating section is recommended to be retained as backup to ensure reliability and operational flexibility.

*Where applicable, IESO and Enbridge incentives for heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics. Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/100-000-enbridge-incentive

measures.existing_conditions: At the present, the building relies on external utilities to provide electricity to power the building which might lead to high electrical energy costs.
measures.notes: Install net metered solar PV generated electricity to offset electricity consumption.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
The current state of the solar industry in Ontario is focused on “net metering” as power export to the grid is no longer an option. Rather than power export, net metered solar facilities use the generated electricity to offset electricity consumption within the facility. Since power export is not feasible, the system should be sized to only meet the baseload energy consumption of the building. This building has a high electrical consumption and ample roof space, which makes it a candidate for solar PV. 

A preliminary study is required to accurately estimate the system cost and savings for a Solar PV system

measures.existing_conditions: The building’s electrical infrastructure is currently operating near or at its available capacity, with limited allowance for additional electrical loads. The existing transformer and distribution system were designed based on historical building demand and may not be adequate to support modern electrification strategies or increased plug and HVAC loads.
measures.notes: Upgrade electrical infrastructure capacity to enable future electrification, including heat pump systems, EV charging, and other high-efficiency electrical upgrades.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends conducting a comprehensive electrical system upgrade strategy to improve the building’s capacity for future electrification and energy-efficiency retrofits. This may include:

Installation of additional transformer capacity or replacement with higher-capacity units
Upgrades to main distribution panels and feeders
Load redistribution and panel balancing
Integration planning for future electrified systems such as air-source heat pumps (ASHP), EV charging infrastructure, and high-efficiency electric equipment

Improving electrical infrastructure capacity will enable the building to transition toward lower-carbon technologies, support future HVAC upgrades, and enhance long-term operational flexibility.

*Further engineering review and detailed feasibility study are required to confirm system capacity, infrastructure constraints, and implementation strategy.

*For additional information regarding electrification strategies and retrofit support, please visit:
https://www.mannengineering.com/ask-an-energy-expert

measures.existing_conditions: Electric vehicle (EV) ownership is expected to grow substantially over the next decade, and many multi-residential and commercial buildings currently lack dedicated EV charging infrastructure for residents, staff, or visitors
measures.notes: Plan and install EV charging infrastructure for residents and staff, contact us for more detail.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Upgrading through the Trade‑In Program is recommended to replace outdated units with OCPP‑networked TAR‑M chargers, providing managed access, usage metering, and load balancing. Early participants benefit from reduced capital cost, including no‑cost upgrades for the first two owners, along with ongoing carbon‑credit rebates of $0.03–$0.05/kWh.

*Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/

misc_items.text:
The building is currently served by an existing electrical transformer rated at approximately 416 V / 75 kVA, which appears undersized relative to current building demand. Based on discussions with the ESA technician, the existing transformer capacity is insufficient to support additional electrical loads, and installation of an additional transformer of similar capacity would be required to accommodate future demand.

This limitation restricts the building’s ability to implement future electrification measures, including but not limited to air-source heat pump (ASHP) retrofits or other electrically driven HVAC system upgrades.
misc_items.title: Electrical Capacity Limitation – Transformer

misc_items.text: The building appears to be served by a single master interval meter, and there is currently no electrical sub-metering system in place to monitor power distribution or track electricity consumption at the individual suite or major end-use level. Based on discussions with site staff, utility costs, including hydro and domestic hot water, are incorporated into common maintenance fees, which suggests that consumption is not individually metered.
misc_items.title: No sub-metering

misc_items.text: The parking garage is served by a mechanical ventilation system controlled by carbon monoxide (CO) sensors. Exhaust fans start and stop in response to measured CO levels, providing demand-based operation and reducing unnecessary runtime during periods of low vehicle activity. The garage fans and control system appeared to be functioning normally, with no obvious mechanical deficiencies reported.
misc_items.title: Garage ventilation (Has CO controls)

misc_items.text: The building envelope appears to be in generally good condition, with no significant signs of air leakage or deterioration observed at the time of the site visit. Envelope components appear to be performing as intended.
misc_items.title: Envelope Condition (Good)

misc_items.text: Lighting throughout the building is generally in good working order. Common areas, corridors, and service spaces appear to be equipped with a mix of LED and fluorescent fixtures. No widespread outages were observed during the walkthrough, and the overall lighting levels were appropriate for the building’s use. Further savings may be available through continued LED retrofit and the use of occupancy-based controls in selected low-traffic areas. Or installing light control in the parking area.
misc_items.title: Lighting condition and controls

misc_items.text: In aging buildings, even double-pane window assemblies may experience gradual deterioration of glazing seals over time. Loss of insulating gas or degradation of the sealed air space between panes can reduce overall thermal performance. While the existing windows were observed to be in generally fair condition, it would be prudent to incorporate sealant renewal and eventual glazing upgrades into the building’s long-term capital planning strategy.
misc_items.title: Window condition (Aging double pane)

misc_items.text: The existing toilets are estimated to operate at approximately 4.8 liters per flush (LPF). Upgrading to modern dual-flush, low-flow toilet fixtures, typically rated at approximately 3.0–3.5 LPF for full flush with reduced volumes for liquid waste, would reduce domestic water consumption and associated sewer charges while maintaining acceptable fixture performance and occupant comfort.
misc_items.title: Toilet Flush (4.8 LPF)

misc_items.text: The building includes an unheated parking garage, which is typical for buildings of this age. No dedicated space-heating system was observed, and garage temperatures are allowed to fluctuate with outdoor conditions.
misc_items.title: Unheated garage

misc_items.text: The exterior ramp heating system is hydronic ramp heating and is used to maintain safe, ice-free conditions during winter months. No operational issues were observed with the ramp heating system at the time of the visit. Control improvements may be possible by converting the electric ramp heating system to a hydronic system, where feasible, to reduce electrical energy consumption while maintaining winter safety performance
misc_items.title: Electric ramp heating

misc_items.text: The building is served by a packaged domestic water booster pump system equipped with variable frequency drives (VFDs). The booster pack modulates pump speed in response to system demand, maintaining stable water pressure throughout the building while reducing unnecessary energy consumption during low-demand periods. The booster pump system was observed to be operating normally at the time of the site visit, with no abnormal noise, vibration, or visible mechanical deficiencies noted
misc_items.title: Has VFD on Booster Pump

misc_items.text: The indoor pool area is served by a dedicated dehumidifer providing ventilation, dehumidification, and space conditioning. The unit is designed to control humidity levels, maintain indoor air quality, and prevent condensation-related deterioration within the pool enclosure
misc_items.title: Pool dehumidifer

misc_items.text: No emergency generator was observed on site. Stairwell emergency lighting is supported by a battery backup system consisting of approximately ten (10) batteries. While this configuration provides basic life-safety lighting during power outages, it does not support extended backup power for other critical building systems.
misc_items.title: No Emergency Generator

misc_items.text: The building is served by aging in suite fuse panels consistent with the original construction era. While the panel appeared to be functional and no immediate safety deficiencies were observed during the site visit, its configuration and capacity reflect outdated electrical standards and may offer limited flexibility to support future electrical loads, energy-efficiency upgrades, or electrification initiatives. Further detailed electrical assessment is recommended prior to implementing major electrical or energy-related retrofits to confirm available capacity, code compliance, and long-term suitability
misc_items.title: Electric Panel (fuse panels)

ventilation_items.text: Ventilation for the building is provided by two (2) make-up air (MUA) units, located in roof top, serving corridors and other public areas.
ventilation_items.title: Rooftop MUA

ventilation_items.text:
The existing make-up air (MUA) unit is equipped with a constant-speed supply fan and an integral gas-fired heating burner, providing heating-only capacity. The unit does not include variable frequency drive (VFD) control and does not provide mechanical cooling.

The absence of VFD control results in fixed airflow operation regardless of actual ventilation demand, limiting part-load efficiency and increasing electrical energy consumption. The gas-fired heating section provides basic winter heating capability; however, without cooling capacity, heat recovery, or advanced modulation control, the system offers limited seasonal optimization and indoor temperature regulation.

At the time of the site visit, the unit was observed to be in functional condition with no visible mechanical deficiencies. However, the configuration reflects an older, conventional ventilation design with limited energy efficiency and control flexibility.
ventilation_items.title: No VFD + Gas Fire (heating only)
